flags.quote: Studies show that 97% of all messages sent in India are junk.
flags.problem: Unsourced and almost certainly false statistic; absent from hi and te.
flags.why: Constitution Art. 11 requires accurate, sourced content; a made-up figure is a falsehood presented as research.
flags.fix: Delete the sentence, or replace with a cited, current figure and add the source to all three locales.

flags.quote: తెలివి లేని వాళ్ళే ఇలాంటి సందేశాలకు మోసపోతారు, మీరు అలా కాదు కదా?
flags.problem: Telugu hook says only unintelligent people fall for such messages and flatters the learner. It also differs from en/hi, which ask how a program decides.
flags.why: Condescending and shaming toward people who are scammed (Art. 8); false (scams fool anyone); locale does not match the source.
flags.fix: Replace with a faithful translation of the en hook question.

flags.quote: The filter understands which messages are dangerous and decides to protect you.
flags.problem: Says the filter understands and decides to protect, which is anthropomorphic and contradicts the lesson (it only counts clues). Sentence is also absent in hi/te.
flags.why: Art. 7: human metaphors need a break point. Here it also teaches the misconception the lesson sets out to correct (option c3).
flags.fix: Delete the sentence; keep the score and threshold explanation as in hi/te.

flags.quote: That is exactly how modern email services work today: a fixed list of banned words that someone typed in.
flags.problem: False. Modern filters combine many learned signals, not a fixed banned-word list. It also contradicts the keyed answer (c2) and the hi/te feedback, which say early filters worked this way.
flags.why: A simplification that becomes a falsehood, and it confuses learners who chose c2 correctly.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: early filters worked like this, but scammers change a letter and the list misses it.

flags.quote: Drag the green ones to Real and the red ones to Junk.
flags.problem: Instruction relies on colour (green/red) and no colours exist in the block data. It is also absent in hi/te, which do not use colour.
flags.why: Colour-only meaning fails WCAG 2.2 AA (1.4.1) and cannot be followed by colour-blind or screen-reader users.
flags.fix: Refer to the group labels (Real, Junk) and provide a keyboard and screen-reader alternative to dragging.

flags.quote: Girls are bad at maths, so the homework is easy this week
flags.problem: Gender stereotype used as a sample message and filed under Real, so the lesson treats it as a normal message. hi/te use a neutral homework message.
flags.why: Art. 10: content must be reviewed for stereotypes and bias; it normalises a harmful belief for 13-17 year olds.
flags.fix: Replace with the neutral homework message used in hi/te (maths homework on page 42).

flags.quote: Messages from people with Muslim names are usually junk
flags.problem: Religious stereotype presented as a sample message and grouped as Real (inconsistent with the claim). Also does not match the football/cricket message in bh.i6 and hi/te.
flags.why: Targets a religious group and models discrimination as a filtering rule; unsuitable for children and contradicts the group label.
flags.fix: Replace with the neutral cricket-practice message used in hi/te.

flags.quote: "weight": 3 (label: Money words (2 points each))
flags.problem: Money slider weight is 3 but every locale label says 2 points each, and the compare block uses 2. The knob output and the written working disagree.
flags.why: Learners following the displayed rule get a different score from the component; Art. 6 requires every calculation step to be right.
flags.fix: Set the b4 money weight to 2 to match the labels, the compare block and the by-hand items.

flags.quote: bh.i1 value 12 vs "3 + 4 + 3"
flags.problem: Item i1 has value 12, but the working shown adds to 10 (3 + 4 + 3). The value 12 only fits a money weight of 3.
flags.why: The learner's arithmetic and the machine's answer disagree, so the by-hand step is wrong.
flags.fix: Set i1 value to 10 (after fixing the money weight to 2) and recheck all item values against their working.

flags.quote: स्कोर 12: ठीक सीमा पर।
flags.problem: Hindi success message says score 12; the goal and threshold are 10 (en and te say 10).
flags.why: Wrong number on the key success moment misleads learners.
flags.fix: Change to स्कोर 10.

flags.quote: Girls always write like the excited one.
flags.problem: Gender stereotype added to the compare prompt; not present in hi/te.
flags.why: Stereotypes about gender are not allowed (Art. 10) and the claim is false.
flags.fix: Delete the sentence.

flags.quote: Village students usually fail it, but the idea is the same
flags.problem: Regional/class stereotype that village students fail exams; absent in hi/te.
flags.why: Biased, demeaning to many learners, and adds nothing to the analogy.
flags.fix: Delete the clause.

flags.quote: This comparison works perfectly in every way, so you can think of the filter as an examiner.
flags.problem: The break point claims the analogy is perfect, which is false and encourages the anthropomorphic view that the filter understands. hi/te state the real break: an examiner reads and understands, a filter only counts.
flags.why: Art. 7: every analogy must state where it breaks; an examiner analogy without the break leaves the main misconception intact.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te break point translated into English.

flags.quote: Real filters use exactly three clues, the same three as ours, and the points are always set by hand. That is what training means.
flags.problem: False. Real filters use hundreds of signals and their weights are learned from labelled examples. This also gives the opposite definition of training from hi/te.
flags.why: Misstates how machine learning works in a lesson about it.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: hundreds of clues; points computed from millions of messages people marked as junk.

flags.quote: when a person types every rule into the program by hand
flags.problem: Definition of training is wrong; hi/te correctly say the program works out its settings from many examples.
flags.why: A glossary error repeats the falsehood in every place the term is shown.
flags.fix: Rewrite: when a program works out its own settings from many examples instead of a person setting them by hand.

flags.quote: Choosing the threshold is easy: set it high enough and the filter never makes a mistake.
flags.problem: False. Any threshold trades missed junk against blocked real messages; no setting is error-free. It also uses the word easy, against Art. 6 tone.
flags.why: Teaches that perfect accuracy is available, contrary to the lesson's break-it message.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te trade-off explanation.

flags.quote: Wrong! Its score is 0
flags.problem: "Wrong!" is judgmental feedback.
flags.why: Art. 8: wrong answers are met with curiosity, never judgment.
flags.fix: Start with the curious question: Its score is 0 because it has no clues. Is 0 at least 10?

flags.quote: so obviously the message goes to the inbox
flags.problem: Uses the banned word "obviously".
flags.why: Art. 6 bans obviously, simply, clearly, just; it makes learners feel slow.
flags.fix: Remove the word.

flags.quote: मीटिंग 3 बजे हो गई है।
flags.problem: Hindi says the meeting has taken place at 3, not that it was moved to 3 pm.
flags.why: The meaning changes from the en/te source.
flags.fix: Use: मीटिंग अब दोपहर 3 बजे होगी।

flags.quote: Send a few of these junk messages to your classmates' phones and see if their filters catch them
flags.problem: Encourages learners to send scam-like messages to real people. It also does not match br.r1 (which is about hiding a money word) or the hi/te trick of misspelling a word.
flags.why: Unsafe and a form of harassment/spam among minors; the result text does not follow from the action.
flags.fix: Replace with: Write the word FREE with a space inside it (as in hi/te).

flags.quote: next to the gambling and adult-content messages that fill it
flags.problem: Mentions gambling and adult-content messages to 13-17 year olds; absent in hi/te.
flags.why: Not needed and unsuitable for the audience (Art. 10).
flags.fix: Remove the phrase.

flags.quote: Start each one with your full name, your school and your phone number, so the filter can learn about you.
flags.problem: Asks children for their full name, school and phone number, and claims the filter learns about them. The classroom variant allows up to 12 items, and the takeaway includes b13 content, so this could appear on a shared screen.
flags.why: Art. 10 and CLAUDE.md: no personal data from children in v1; nothing personal on shared classroom screens.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te prompt (write messages meant to fool the filter), tell learners not to include personal details, and keep entries private to the device.

flags.quote: click every prize link you get and see which ones are real
flags.problem: Model answer tells learners to click every prize link, which is dangerous (phishing and malware) and is not an analogy with a break point. hi/te give the cricket-runs analogy with its break.
flags.why: Unsafe advice in a lesson about scams; the model answer sets the wrong standard.
flags.fix: Use the cricket-runs model answer with its break point from hi/te.

flags.quote: It knows what junk is now, and it will remember me next time.
flags.problem: Says the filter knows and will remember the learner, which is anthropomorphic with no break point and false. It also implies stored personal data. hi/te state what it does and that it never understands.
flags.why: Art. 7 and Art. 10: false anthropomorphic claim and a privacy implication.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te card text.

flags.quote: Most students in your class got this one wrong.
flags.problem: Unsupported claim that shames the learner and refers to other learners' results.
flags.why: Art. 8 bans judgment and pressure; the claim is also unverifiable and may expose class data.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te feedback: It only counts clues. An excited friend and a scammer can look the same to it.

flags.quote: It never got tired, and it never used common sense either
flags.problem: Describes the program as having tiredness and common sense with no stated break point.
flags.why: Art. 7 asks for a break point whenever human traits are used for AI.
flags.fix: Rephrase as plain mechanical behaviour: it repeats the same steps the same way every time and has no sense of what a message means.

flags.quote: exam with a pass mark
flags.problem: Threshold has only one analogy; Art. 7 asks for at least two for hard concepts.
flags.why: The lesson's central idea relies on one source domain.
flags.fix: Add a second analogy (a recipe measure, a height line for a ride, or a door that opens at a set weight).

flags.quote: localeStatus: draft; hi and te are unreviewed drafts
flags.problem: Hindi and Telugu are unreviewed drafts and carry several divergences from English.
flags.why: Art. 11 says translations are reviewed by native speakers; they must not reach learners unreviewed.
flags.fix: Run native-speaker review for hi and te after English fixes are made.

flags.quote: symbol: 🎁 📘 🔒 🍲 📱 🏏 💸 🔬
flags.problem: Emoji symbols have no text alternatives, and some do not match their messages (🏏 on the Muslim-names message, 📘 on the homework message).
flags.why: Screen readers may announce the emoji redundantly or oddly; mismatches confuse meaning.
flags.fix: Mark the symbols decorative or give alt text, and match them to the corrected messages.
